forge-mat.basis: 280 cm³ × 0.00785 kg/cm³ (steel, confirmed by engineer); steel → 38MnVS6 (Microalloyed) (representative forging billet — not a drawing callout); the STEP product name ("HUB FLANGE FORGING C45 2") names C45 / 1045 / CK45 (medium-carbon forging steel) — costed as 38MnVS6 (Microalloyed) until the grade question is answered (a name leans the question; it does not set the grade)

forge-part-wt.basis: 2.198 kg finished + 16.6 cm³ of holes drilled from solid (≤ Ø25; larger bores pierced) + 49.1 cm³ machining stock (1.5 mm a side on the machined faces — IS 3469 (Part I):1974 Table 1.5 minimum finish stock for a drop / press forging whose greatest dimension (140.0 mm) is not over 205 mm) + 31.9 cm³ turning stock on the 160 cm² turned axis (2 mm a side, engineering-typical, not sourced) + 28.1 cm³ draft metal (draft metal 28.1 cm³ = Σ A·h·tan α / 2 over the 3 zero-draft face(s) along the Z parting axis (parting at the mid-plane of the part's extent, 25.0 mm — CostVision approximation): inside ≤ 25 mm 1 face(s), 9,425 mm², Σ A·h 235,620 mm³ at 7°: 235620 × 0.12278 ÷ 2 ÷ 1000 = 14.46 cm³; outside ≤ 25 mm 2 face(s), 15,959 mm², Σ A·h 311,898 mm³ at 5°: 311898 × 0.08749 ÷ 2 ÷ 1000 = 13.64 cm³ — α the lower end of IS 3469 (Part I):1974 Table 1.4 normal drafts (outside 5–7° / 5–10°, inside 7–10° / 8–12°, depth ≤ 25 / > 25 mm); inside = the face's outward normal meets the part again (one ray); exact for a plane face, a cylinder on its developed area; holes drilled from solid excluded) = 2.198 kg + 125.7 cm³ × 0.00785 kg/cm³ = 3.185 kg — 280 cm³ × 0.00785 kg/cm³ (steel, confirmed by engineer)

forge-proj-area.basis: largest of the three measured silhouettes — a forging parts round its largest periphery

forge-shape.basis: score 0 + 0 + 0 = 0 → simple — 0 for 0 free-form face(s), 0 for 0 undercut face(s), 0 for 12 faces (≥ 3 complex, ≥ 1 moderate; free-form ≥ 3 / ≥ 8, undercuts ≥ 4, faces ≥ 120 — CostVision heuristic)

forge-yield.basis: closed-die stock yield band 0.55–0.8, midpoint 0.675 — as-forged weight ÷ billet, CostVision engineering-typical, not sourced; the 10% flash is itemised, so yieldFraction = 0.675 × 1.10 = 0.743; billet = 3.185 kg forging + 0.319 kg flash = 3.504 kg ÷ 0.743 = 4.716 kg; finished ÷ billet = 2.198 kg ÷ 4.716 kg = 0.47; 4.716 − 3.504 = 1.212 kg is scale, crop and any pierced wad (not itemised)

forge-flash.basis: 10% of the 3.185 kg forging, squeezed out at the flash land (CostVision engineering-typical, not sourced) — cost-neutral: the yield is scaled by the same fraction, so the billet stays forging ÷ 0.675

forge-mach.basis: Kt 3 for a simple shape, σflow 105 MPa hot flow stress for microalloyed-steel (both CostVision engineering-typical, not sourced); A = 116 cm² silhouette + 22.97 cm² flash land = 138.97 cm²; F = Kt × σflow × A = 3 × 105 MPa × 13,897 mm² ÷ 9,806.65 N/t = 446 t × 1.2 safety = 535 t → the smallest forge press at or above it: the 1,600 t press (library presses 500, 1,600, 2,500, 4,000, 8,000 t)

forge-strokes.basis: 2 hit(s): 2 impression(s); takt = 3 s billet from the heater + 2 × 4 s mechanical press hit + transfer = 11 s (load and hit times CostVision engineering-typical, not sourced)

forge-time-per-blow.basis: hit + transfer on the press (informational — the cycle below is the line takt)

forge-ct.basis: 2 hit(s): 2 impression(s); takt = 3 s billet from the heater + 2 × 4 s mechanical press hit + transfer = 11 s (load and hit times CostVision engineering-typical, not sourced). The billet cut-off and the induction heater are their own operations (billetSaw…, billetHeater…)

forge-manning.basis: closed-die line crew: forger + heater / handler — engineering typical

forge-reject.basis: 2% forging scrap (laps, underfill, cracks at inspection) — engineering typical

forge-furnace.basis: steel / titanium billets for an impression line heat in-line by induction

forge-saw-mach.basis: billet cut off the bar on the automatic carbide saw (billet 4.716 kg cut from round bar at a height / diameter of 2.3 (the free-upset limit, CostVision heuristic) = Ø69.3 mm; kerf π/4 × 69.3² mm² × 3 mm (engineering-typical carbide kerf, not sourced) × 7.85 g/cm³ = 0.0888 kg)

forge-saw-ct.basis: 1 ÷ 400 cuts an hour = 0.0025 h a billet — ENGINEERING ESTIMATE (no published cut time for this bar was found)

forge-saw-manning.basis: one operator tends two automatic saws — ENGINEERING ESTIMATE, not sourced

forge-saw-kerf.basis: billet 4.716 kg cut from round bar at a height / diameter of 2.3 (the free-upset limit, CostVision heuristic) = Ø69.3 mm; kerf π/4 × 69.3² mm² × 3 mm (engineering-typical carbide kerf, not sourced) × 7.85 g/cm³ = 0.0888 kg — bought as bar, lost in the cut, credited as scrap

forge-heater-mach.basis: the in-line induction billet heater (~500 kW, SMS Elotherm sizing); fed by the forge crew — no crew of its own; its energy is the per-kg heating line, not in its machine rate

forge-heater-ct.basis: 4.716 kg billet ÷ 1,250 kg/h = 0.00377 h a billet — the heater's throughput, SMS Elotherm (~500 kW to 1,250 °C, a maker's claim for billets ≤ Ø51 mm; a larger billet heats slower — not adjusted)

forge-trim-mach.basis: flash line 4.4 √A = 474 mm and flash 0.015 √A = 1.62 mm over A = 11,600 mm² (outline and thickness after ASM closed-die practice); 474 mm × 1.62 mm × 105 MPa hot flow stress ÷ 9,806.65 N/t = 8.2 t × 1.25 margin = 10.25 t → the 100 t press, the smallest mechanical press in the library at or above it (flow stress CostVision engineering-typical, not sourced; a pierce in the same stroke is not added to the force)

forge-trim-ct.basis: the trim press stands in line and works to the forge takt (11 s)

forge-trim-manning.basis: one operator on the in-line trim press

forge-die-cost.basis: 2-impression h13 die over 116 cm²: Die design & CAM 41.9 h £2,447 + Die blocks (both halves + holder allowance) 160 kg £1,523 + Block prep (squaring, faces, keyways) 38 h £1,991 + Die sinking × 2 impression(s) 145.9 h £7,639 + EDM (deep ribs, tight radii) 29.2 h £1,704 + Harden + temper the blocks £2,853 + Impression polishing × 2 25.6 h £1,160 + Die tryout — 3 sessions 18 h £1,541 = £20,858; toolmaker overhead + profit at 22% of it = £4,589; die set £20,858 + £4,589 = £25,447 (toolroom hours and the die-block rules are CostVision engineering-typical, not sourced; rates from the toolroom book)

forge-die-life.basis: size factor (100 ÷ 116 cm²)^0.2 = 0.970752; 38,000 forgings a die set for microalloyed steel × 1.3 simple impression × 0.970752 size = 47,955 forgings — CostVision engineering-typical figures, not sourced; die sets are charged fractionally over the programme

forge-heat-energy.basis: energy to bring microalloyed-steel to forging temperature in the in-line induction heater: 500 kW ÷ 1,250 kg/h = 0.4 kWh/kg (SMS Elotherm, a maker's claim for steel billets ≤ Ø51 mm to 1,250 °C); charged on every billet heated: 0.4 kWh/kg × 4.716 kg billet ÷ 0.98 for the 2% scrap = 1.925 kWh a good part, priced at the costing book's tariff as kWh (gas furnace × 2.4 kWh of gas)

forge-ht-cost.basis: none — a microalloyed-steel forging is controlled-cooled from the forge heat (no separate heat treatment). The file names C45 / 1045 / CK45 (medium-carbon forging steel): a carbon-steel forging is normalised — £0.3/kg × 3.185 kg = £0.9555 a part before overhead and margin, NOT in this cost until the grade question is answered

forge-descale.basis: forge scale removed after the trim, before MPI and machining (shot blast or pickle): £0.12/kg × the 3.185 kg forging — the flash is off by then — UK price × the country's process-service factor, CostVision engineering-typical, not sourced

forge-sf-route.basis: not asked yet — costed bare (answer "Is the part coated?" to price a finish)

forge-sf-area.basis: measured surface 534.2 cm² = 0.0534 m² — the whole wetted surface; a masked or machined-after-coating face is in it
